title: How Redis Makes Apps Fast: Caching in 60 Seconds ⚡ #shorts
description:
Why does a page load in 2 seconds the first time and instantly the next? Caching. Databases store data on disk and run queries, often 100+ ms. Redis keeps hot data in RAM as simple key-value pairs, answering in under a millisecond. Apps check Redis first: on a cache hit they return instantly, on a miss they query the database and save the result with a TTL so it expires, keeping data fresh. The hard part: invalidating the cache when the data changes.

Times shown are typical, illustrative values.

lines: Why does a page take two seconds to load the first time, and load instantly the next?
Caching. And the most popular cache is Redis.
A database stores data on disk, and has to run a query every time. That can take a hundred milliseconds or more.
Redis keeps data in memory, in RAM, as simple key-value pairs. Reading from it takes less than a millisecond.
So your app checks Redis first. If the data is there, that's a cache hit, and it's returned instantly.
If not, that's a cache miss. The app asks the database, then saves the answer in Redis, so the next request is fast.
Each cached value gets a TTL, a time to live, so it expires and gets refreshed. Because the hardest part of caching is stale data.
Check the cache. Fall back to the database. Save for next time.
